messages.author: 9fb3ae5e7320102b
messages.subject: thinning data
parts:
Hi Chris,
We have automated telemetry data for birds, sampled continuously (day and night) at fairly high temporal resolution (every 2-5 mins)...with occasional gaps in detection when birds are in dense vegetation, or briefly outside the telemetry array. Between ~20 and 60% of our detections occur at night for these birds, depending on individual. Previous studies estimating home ranges for diurnal birds do not typically have information on nocturnal locations. We are thinking of either removing nocturnal location estimates, or thinning them to one random detection per hour. We are concerned that the high temporal resolution of nocturnal detections while individuals are largely stationary will "drown out" the signal of space use during the day. A quick analysis looking at HR estimates for a few birds with and without the nocturnal detections reveals that when we include nocturnal detections 1) the HR area estimates are lower, 2) the tau position estimates are larger, and 3) the shape of the HR changes. A review of the literature confirms that many data sets from GPS/Argos trackers simply do not collect data while individuals are inactive, so there is some precedent for leaving out the nocturnal detections. I wonder however, whether we might be potentially introducing some bias by removing or thinning nocturnal detections? What are your thoughts or recommendations on this matter?

In case this influences the matter, we are incorporating estimates of error in the modeling process, based on calibration data from transmitters at known locations.

Thank you!
Jenny

messages.author: 40fd627580dd34f5
messages.subject: Re: thinning data
parts:
Hi Jenny,

If you have two behavioral states on a diurnal species like this, then its probably not good to fit one stationary movement model to both behavior states. The first thing you would want to do is segment the data and fit separate movement models. Further complications might warrant even more data wrangling: like is the nocturnal behavior centered on one nest or does it vary, etc..

With two behavioral states, there are really two distinct distributions with two different meanings, and where the nocturnal distribution is much smaller than the day distribution. I would estimate these distributions separately with their separate movement models (and separate/segmented data). The more important range is probably the larger diurnal range, but you might also want to report the daily/aggregate range by averaging the two with mean() and appropriate weights argument (https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/mean.html).

Best,
Chris
